title: The Perceptron, 1958, and exactly why XOR broke it in 1969
story:
Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, described the perceptron in Psychological Review in 1958. The machine built to embody it was an analogue device wired to an array of 400 photocells. The unit itself is simple: a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through a threshold — which means, geometrically, that it divides its input space with a single hyperplane and answers according to which side a point falls on.

The reception was not simple. The New York Times reported the Navy's announcement on 8 July 1958, describing the embryo of an electronic computer that the Navy expected would be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.

Then Minsky and Papert published Perceptrons: An Introduction to Computational Geometry in 1969, establishing what a single-layer perceptron cannot compute. Exclusive-or is the standard example and it is worth seeing rather than accepting. Four input combinations: the two matching pairs give one answer, the two mismatched pairs give the other. Plot them and the two classes sit on opposite diagonals of a square. A single straight line has to put two corners on one side and two on the other, and the pairs that need separating are the diagonals — so no line does it, which means no setting of weights and bias for one threshold unit computes it. This is not a training difficulty. The function is not in the model's range at all.

That is a clean, correct and permanent result about one layer. What happened to it afterwards is the part this lesson exists to correct.

The received story is that the book proved neural networks were a dead end, funding vanished, and the field went dark for fifteen years. That causal claim is contested, and Olazaran's 1996 study in Social Studies of Science is the canonical scholarly treatment of the dispute. The revisionist case has several strands: Minsky and Papert had been arguing against neural networks since around 1965, in talks and preprints, so the book was a culmination rather than an opening shot; its mathematical content concerns single-layer perceptrons rather than all neural networks; many researchers had already left the area by 1969, out of frustration at the lack of progress; and Rosenblatt died in 1971. The position most often defended is weaker than the popular one — that the critique, combined with its authors' standing, exerted significant influence in temporarily stalling neural network research in the United States.

The dates do not fit the story either. The first funding collapse is associated with the mid-1970s rather than with 1969, and followed the 1973 Lighthill report and the Department of Defense American Study Group report, after which funding decreased sharply in both countries. A book published four years earlier is part of a climate, not a trigger.

So the honest version is more useful than the myth, and the two things worth separating are these. The mathematical result is correct, and its scope is one layer. The historical claim — that this result killed the field — is a strong causal statement about a complicated period, attached to a tidy narrative, repeated far more confidently than the evidence supports. That the misreading happened at all is the more interesting fact: a precise result about single-layer perceptrons was widely received as a result about neural networks in general, and the gap between those two statements did real damage.

The fix, once it existed, is also precise. Add a hidden layer with a non-linear activation, and the earlier layers transform the input space so that a linear boundary in the final layer suffices. The non-linearity is not decoration: composing linear maps yields a linear map, so a hundred stacked linear layers compute exactly what one computes. Without the non-linear step, depth buys nothing at all.

problem.name: Representable versus learnable
problem.shape: A model fails at a task, and the question is whether it was trained badly or cannot express the answer.
tell: a model fails identically regardless of training time or data
the decision boundary the task needs is not the shape the model draws
a limitation of one configuration is being discussed as a limitation of a family
a historical narrative explains a field's direction with a single cause
problem.move: Separate what the model can represent from what training can find. Where a function is outside the model's range no amount of optimisation reaches it, so the remedy is a change of architecture — and when reading limits, check whether the proof's scope is the configuration or the whole family.
problem.invariant: One threshold unit divides its input space with a single hyperplane, so any function whose classes are not separable by one hyperplane cannot be computed by it at any weights.
problem.breaks: The result is about one layer, and it was received as being about neural networks generally. That misreading, not the theorem, is what the popular history attributes to the book — and the historical causal claim itself is contested, since the funding collapse followed 1973 reports rather than the 1969 publication.

cost.time: depth makes the optimisation harder and was not trainable in practice for years after the limitation was understood
cost.space: hidden layers add parameters that are not interpretable individually, which is part of why the approach was resisted
cost.beats: engineering features by hand so that the classes become separable, which works and requires knowing the answer in advance, and other model families with convex training and provable bounds, which is what the field turned to

worked.problem: Why can a single-layer perceptron not compute exclusive-or, and what removes the limitation?
worked.reasoning:
Because one threshold unit divides its input space with a single hyperplane, and the two classes of exclusive-or cannot be put on opposite sides of any one line.

Work it rather than assert it. There are four input combinations. The two matching pairs give one answer and the two mismatched pairs give the other, so plotted on a square the two classes occupy opposite diagonals. A straight line splits the square into two parts; to separate the classes it would have to place both matching corners on one side and both mismatched corners on the other, and those pairs are diagonals of the square, which no line separates.

The distinction that makes this worth knowing generally is between representable and learnable. This is not a training failure — there is no learning rate, no amount of data and no patience that helps, because no weights and bias exist that compute the function. It is outside the model's range entirely, and that is a different kind of failure from a model that could express the answer and has not found it.

The remedy is a hidden layer with a non-linear activation. The earlier layer transforms the input space so that the classes become separable by a linear boundary in the final layer. The non-linearity is the essential part and I would stress why: composing linear maps gives a linear map, so a hundred stacked linear layers compute exactly what one layer computes. Without the non-linear step, depth buys literally nothing.

The history is worth handling carefully, because the usual telling contains a causal claim stronger than the evidence. Minsky and Papert published the result in 1969, and the received story is that it proved neural networks were a dead end, funding vanished, and the field went dark for fifteen years. That is contested — Olazaran's 1996 study is the canonical scholarly treatment. The revisionist strands: the authors had been arguing against neural networks since around 1965, so the book was a culmination rather than an opening shot; its content concerns single-layer perceptrons, not all neural networks; many researchers had already left out of frustration at the lack of progress by 1969; and Rosenblatt died in 1971. The defensible version is weaker — that the critique, combined with its authors' standing, exerted significant influence in temporarily stalling the research in the United States.

The dates do not support the tidy story either. The first funding collapse is associated with the mid-1970s and followed the 1973 Lighthill report and the Department of Defense study, not the 1969 publication.

What I would take from the episode is the thing that is actually well-evidenced and more interesting than the myth: a precise result about single-layer perceptrons was widely received as a result about the whole approach. The theorem's scope and its reception were different, and the gap between them did real damage — which is a better lesson about reading limitations than any story about one book ending a field.

problem.practice: Draw the four exclusive-or points on paper and try to separate them with a straight line. Then add one intermediate feature of your own invention and check that a line now works — that feature is what a hidden unit learns.

beats.broke: A model was promoted as an artificial brain on the strength of what it could learn, with nobody having characterised what it could not represent at any weights.
beats.fix: Establish the limit formally — one threshold unit divides its input space with a single hyperplane — then add a hidden layer with a non-linear activation so earlier layers reshape the space until a linear boundary suffices.
beats.cost: The result was about one layer and was widely received as being about the whole approach, and the popular history of what followed is a stronger causal claim than the evidence supports.

interview.answer:

Work it: four input combinations, the matching pairs giving one answer and the mismatched pairs the other. Plotted on a square, the classes occupy opposite diagonals.
